title: The virtuous elephant
hookLine: an elephant rescues a lost man, who comes back to saw off his tusks (Jataka 72)
tomorrow: The fish who prayed for rain

lines: A MAN LOST IN THE FOREST.
cards: A man from Benares has gone into the forest for work and lost his way. He wanders, crying out in fear. Then a huge white elephant steps out of the trees.
The man runs. The elephant stops. The man stops.
The elephant steps forward; the man runs again. At last the man understands: this animal means no harm. He's the bodhisatta, the tale says, and he's come to help.

teach.b: First, the rescue. The elephant takes the man home, feeds him on fruit, and carries him on his back out of the forest to the road. But as they go, the man quietly notes every tree and hill along the way.

teach.h: THE STREET OF THE IVORY CARVERS.
teach.b: Back in Benares, he walks down the street of the ivory carvers and asks what they'd pay for the tusks of a living elephant. A lot, they say. So he takes a saw and goes back.
Third, the gift. He tells the elephant he's poor, with nothing to live on. Would he give him his tusks?
The elephant kneels and lets him saw. He gives them freely, saying it isn't that he doesn't value them: the wisdom he is seeking is dearer to him. The man sells them, then comes back for the stumps.
Then he comes a third time and digs out the roots of the tusks. Each time, the elephant lets him. Fourth, the end.
As the man walks away, the tale says, the earth splits open and swallows him.
A tree spirit speaks a verse: give an ungrateful man the whole world, and it still won't satisfy him. The tale never calls the elephant foolish.
He gives three times, each gift costing more, and the tale saves its judgment for the taker. The man's ingratitude doesn't get to decide who the elephant is.
The tale's last line names the man as Devadatta, whose ingratitude toward the Buddha is the story's frame.

how: Buddhist teachers tell the Silavanaga Jataka as a picture of generosity and patience that don't depend on gratitude, and as a warning about where ingratitude leads.

games.q: the virtuous elephant: tap the pairs.
p: carried the lost man out of the forest
noted every tree and hill on the way
would pay for a living elephant's tusks
said the whole world won't satisfy him

s: the tale calls the elephant a fool for giving
it never does; it saves its judgment for the man who kept taking.
the man came back three times
first for the tusks, then for the stumps, then for the roots.
the tale names the man in a past life of Devadatta
its last line identifies him as Devadatta.

games.q: you're the elephant. the man you carried out of the forest is back with a saw, asking for your tusks. what do you do?
o: drive him off. you saved his life once already.
kneel and let him take them.
give him fruit instead and send him home.
games.why: the elephant kneels and lets him saw, saying the wisdom he seeks is dearer to him than tusks, and gives again each time he returns.

practice: Remember a time someone took your help and gave nothing back; not the deepest wound you carry, a small one. Forgiving isn't approving, so just see if you can set the weight of it down for a moment, the way the elephant knelt.
Breathe out, and let your kindness belong to you, not to them.

wordCard.voice: Sila. Virtue, good conduct: what the virtuous elephant showed, rescuing a lost man, then giving him tusks, stumps and roots, and staying good to the end. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sila: virtue, good conduct. the tale's name, Silavanaga, means the virtuous elephant.

carryVoice: Your line: good to the ungrateful. The week in lines: dig once more, from a dead mouse, the dance cost him, honor the eldest, the crab remembers, don't pull up the roots. Day eight hundred twenty-six, done.
